newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EMU pact highlights power struggle over economy.
newsitem.headline: EMU pact highlights power struggle over economy.

text.p: Europe's battle over how to curb state spending offers a glimpse of the power struggle which lies ahead over who will shape economic policy under a single currency from 1999.

European Union leaders crowned their summit meeting which ended in Dublin on Saturday with an agreement to give ministers a say on whether to fine nations which borrow heavily within the bloc's planned economic and monetary union (EMU).
There was never any disagreement that the 15-nation bloc had to do more to deter EMU member states from overspending.

But the sharp differences which emerged over how to achieve this highlighted fundamental differences over whether there should be a political counterweight to the independent European Central Bank which will decide monetary policy within EMU.
For months, German-led demands for a stability pact to enforce budget discipline were endorsed in principle but criticised over their stringent terms.

Many of the original proposals, such as the idea of automatic fines, raised fears among EU governments that they would be surrendering power to decide national spending needs. They protested that such a surrender of sovereignty was not envisaged in the Maastricht Treaty, the blueprint for EMU.

The compromise that finally emerged in Dublin Castle on Friday reaffirmed that EU finance ministers will have the power to make a political judgement on whether to fine governments which run annual deficits of more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Summing up the marathon talks this weekend, Irish Finance Minister told reporters, "This was a philosophical and ideological debate about sovereignty."
The group endorsed a pact that would fine governments an initial 0.2 percent of national output if they failed to bring their finances under control, with a maximum penalty of 0.5 percent of GDP.
Countries suffering a sharp downturn, with their economies shrinking by an annual two percent, would be let off the hook.

Governments could also plead their overspending was forced on them by "exceptional circumstances" if the economy shrank by 0.75 percent or more. But in that case, the burden of proof would fall on the offending government to demonstrate why the downturn was out of the ordinary.

The deal went part of the way towards allaying Germany's distrust of its partners' will to maintain fiscal rigour, but it stopped well short of a mechanistic approach that would remove political discretion.
France, a country long-wedded to interventionist economic policies, was the primary advocate of a political accord that enshrined the power of government ministers.
Some economists saw the argument for retaining such flexibility as laudable, particularly given the single-minded mandate of the future European Central Bank to curb inflation.

Automatic penalties for overspending would have further limited the options governments will have under EMU in smoothing the ups and downs of their economies. Under EMU, they will no longer be able to devalue their currencies or print money to get themselves out of trouble.

On top of that, there are still many barriers, including language, which prevent EU workers from moving to another state to find work if their own country hits recession. So any unforeseen economic crisis might in practice only be cushioned by state borrowing.
But the stability pact may turn out to be just the start of a fierce debate over how economic policy will be shaped under EMU.
French President Jacques Chirac on Saturday raised the idea of greater coordination among heads of state on future economic policy.

But he cannot push this idea too far without running up against the German-inspired Maastricht mandate for the European Central Bank, which explicitly rules out any scope for political influence over monetary policy making.

France and Germany, which up to now have been steadfast in their vision of how a single currency will be put in place, showed signs of friction this weekend which may cause financial markets occasional bouts of worry.
Yet as the debate over a budget stability pact showed, the Maastricht treaty may constrain the efforts of either to stray too far in one direction or another.
